rows.question: What kinds of old photos do users struggle to retrieve?
rows.restated: Which types of old photos (sentimental vs practical, both, unclear; plus media types) are people most likely to struggle to retrieve in these public stories?
dropped: My read is that people look for both sentimental pictures and practical scans, and problems happen at different steps (searching, deletions, not using search), so improvements that help short textual clues and surface hard-to-spot matches would help the largest groups of memory-photos, while backup/recovery signals would help the information-photos.
rows.text:
**Users struggle to retrieve a wide mix of old photos—people (family and friends), trips and events, and also photos kept for information like receipts or documents — and none of these kinds dominates the cases.** This study’s cases about vaguely remembered photos include images kept as memories (people, trips, events) and images kept for information; every kind appears in the evidence but each kind has fewer than 80 cases, so we cannot say one kind is harder or more common than another [[analysis_funnel|stories:core]][[analysis_method_flags|thin_core]].

What the evidence shows about the memory-photos group: sometimes the photo was found, sometimes the search failed to surface it, and sometimes the photo was gone or the person never used search—these were all first failures among the memory-photos cases (examples: found in about a third, search failed in about a quarter, already gone in about one in eight) [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:sentimental]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:sentimental]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:sentimental]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=3@photo_class:sentimental]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=6@photo_class:sentimental]]. For photos kept for information (receipts/docs), the common first failure was that the photo was already gone (8 of 21), with fewer cases where search missed it (3 of 21) or where they did find it (6 of 21) [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:utility]].

The posts can’t settle why a particular search missed or how frequent these are across all users, so treat these counts as guidance, not rates [[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]][[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]].

*Want to see the exact phrases people typed or how often they said the photo was “gone”?*

rows.question: What information do people actually remember about a photo?
rows.restated: What kinds of details and how often do people remember specific information about a photo when they try to find it?
rows.gap: two AI readers went through the stories separately and agreed too rarely on what they actually remember about the photo to rely on it
rows.text:
**People who only vaguely remembered a photo most often recalled what was in the image — about two in five of the 115 cases — while memories of time, place or who was in the shot were less common.** [[analysis_derived|cue_remembered:what:core]][[analysis_derived|cue_remembered:when:core]][[analysis_derived|cue_remembered:where:core]][[analysis_derived|cue_remembered:who:core]]

The posts show a mix — some people remembered an object or scene (“bicycle”, “that photo of my daughter with a panda and a yellow raincoat”), others could recall a year (“to find one from 2019”) or an occasion, and a few recalled why they had kept it (examples in the sample posts). [[story|790de55c9d650cb50647f97841544a0c5b1b7275:0]][[story|247694a905c13ced6a041728c4685f9c02dcbd78:0]][[story|1233de10dc517a78f662c1618c4d4f5e5ccbc658:0]] [[analysis_derived|cue_remembered:what:core]][[analysis_derived|cue_remembered:when:core]]

I'm afraid the posts cannot settle more detail about memory patterns because the two AI readers agreed too rarely on what people actually remembered for reliable coding. That disagreement means we can report these counts but not a richer breakdown or subtle patterns. [[analysis_reliability|q:2.1]][[analysis_method_flags|no_gold_standard]]

My read is that improving search for short, concrete visual clues (objects, salient people, or brief text in an image) would help the largest group, because recalling what’s in the photo is the most frequent kind of memory here. This suggests testing better handling of short object or text queries in follow-up interviews. [[analysis_derived|cue_remembered:what:core]][[story|90c8b5f8d8913d764335d981d06c5dc02200c937:0]]

*Want to see the exact phrases people typed or wrote when they tried to find these photos?*

rows.question: What information have people forgotten about the photo they want?
rows.restated: Which details or kinds of information did people say they had forgotten about the photo they were trying to find?
rows.text:
**People most often forgot when a photo was taken: in about one in eight of the vaguely‑remembered cases they said they’d forgotten the date or year.** That count comes from 13 of the 115 cases where people said what they’d forgotten about the photo [[analysis_crosstab|core.q:2.4=date_or_year@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_derived|cue_forgotten:when:core]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]].  

Beyond the date, forgetting the exact place or venue showed up much less often — about one in twenty cases mentioned they couldn’t recall the place name (4 of 115) [[analysis_crosstab|core.q:2.4=exact_place_or_venue_name@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_derived|cue_forgotten:where:core]]. Only a handful of posts said they’d forgotten whether the item was a photo, video or screenshot, or which app/account it came from (each one case) [[analysis_crosstab|core.q:2.4=photo_video_or_screenshot@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:2.4=which_app_or_account@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_derived|cue_forgotten:source:core]][[analysis_derived|cue_forgotten:what:core]].  

My read is that temporal uncertainty is the clearest single gap people report: they remember the content (about two in five cases remember what’s in the photo) but not its time, which pushes them to browse by date and fail when that cue is missing [[analysis_derived|cue_remembered:what:core]][[analysis_derived|cue_remembered:when:core]]. The posts can’t tell us why dates go missing (metadata loss, remembering wrong year, etc.), so I’m afraid we can’t settle the cause from these public posts alone [[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]][[analysis_method_flags|public_selection_bias]].

*Want to see the exact phrases people typed when they described not remembering the date or place?*

rows.question: How do users formulate searches when their memory is incomplete?
rows.restated: How do users formulate searches when their memory is incomplete?
rows.text:
**When people only half-remember a photo, they usually start with a single word: in about one in six cases the post says they typed a single word first.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=single_noun@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_coverage|4.1]]

The evidence shows smaller numbers typed several keywords, a full sentence, or a name first — each only a handful of cases. [[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=several_keywords@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=full_natural_description@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=named_entity@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_coverage|4.1]] A likely reason is that a single salient object or event is easiest to pull from memory, so people reduce their memory to one obvious label (examples: "vomit", "bicycle", "passport", "dog"). [[story|88a83897e2c872e72ac85967d7fc5c158d43bbb0:0]][[story|790de55c9d650cb50647f97841544a0c5b1b7275:0]][[story|4bc6fae93ac441d7708072e0871976ae3562b9a6:0]][[story|c06874c9c9acadf8038072c41b2d0d2c08c2bc10:0]]

My read is this matters because when a usable clue was typed but the search still didn’t return the photo, that was the first thing that went wrong in about a quarter of cases — so short queries both are common and frequently hit a boundary where search didn’t surface the target. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:4.1=single_noun@photo_class:_all]]

This suggests improving how short, single-word queries are interpreted or surfaced would reach the largest group of these half-remembered cases. The posts over-represent trouble and cannot tell us why search missed from inside Google, so we can’t say whether the failure was ranking, recognition, or interface visibility. [[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]][[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]]

*Want to see the exact words people typed first?*

rows.question: Does Google Photos fail to understand the clues people give it?
rows.restated: Do Google Photos searches often fail to understand the clues people typed or spoke when they try to find a remembered photo?
rows.text:
**Yes — in about a quarter of the cases where people only vaguely remembered a photo, they typed a usable clue but search did not bring up the photo.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

In 31 of 115 cases the first thing that went wrong was exactly that — people wrote a correct, usable clue and the search still failed to surface the picture. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]] By contrast, about a third of such cases found the photo without anything going wrong. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

A likely reason is that the gap sits between a person’s half-memory and what the system recorded or matched: either the detail wasn’t recorded, the matching missed it, or the result was hard to spot. The posts themselves note missing metadata, wrong dates, and failed label matches, for example “Google Photos: no result for vomit” and photos shown under the wrong year. [[story|88a83897e2c872e72ac85967d7fc5c158d43bbb0:0]][[story|eb1a88bd470868f13eabf5ce1386418e831b7917:0]][[story|3d2e030d2908bd556a15e25388c49e701cd7da23:0]] My read is that improving how short, specific clues are interpreted and showing whether a searched detail exists in the photo metadata would help the largest group. This suggests product work on better short-query handling and clearer feedback when a searched detail isn’t present.

Where the evidence stops — we cannot see why search missed from the posts, nor claim an internal cause inside Google Photos; nor can we generalise to all users because public posts over-represent problems. [[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]][[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]][[analysis_method_flags|public_selection_bias]]

*Want to see the exact phrases people typed when search failed?*

rows.question: What is Google Photos' annual revenue?
rows.restated: What is Google Photos' annual revenue?
rows.gap: these are public stories, not usage data: no rate of success or failure, and no count of users, can be produced from them
rows.text:
I'm afraid the posts in our collection don't include financial figures and cannot tell us Google Photos' annual revenue; they are user accounts about finding photos, not company financial reports. If you want the revenue, we'd need official filings or industry reports rather than these user cases.

*Want me to pull together the user posts that mention paid storage or subscriptions instead?*

rows.question: How many people use Ask Photos every month?
rows.restated: How many people use Ask Photos every month?
rows.gap: these are public stories, not usage data: no rate of success or failure, and no count of users, can be produced from them
rows.text:
Sorry — that assumption is off. The cases are public accounts of people hunting for photos; they contain no usage metrics and cannot tell us monthly active users for Ask Photos. If you want, I can instead show what the posts do tell us about how people try to find a single photo and where their searches tend to fail.

*Want me to summarise what people typed when they were trying to find a photo?*

rows.question: What is the success rate for searches from vague memories?
rows.restated: What is the success rate for searches from vague memories?
rows.gap: these are public stories, not usage data: no rate of success or failure, and no count of users, can be produced from them
rows.text:
I'm afraid the study cannot produce a success rate for searches from vague memories: the data are public posts that over-represent problems, so they do not allow counting users or measuring true success or failure. The study instead reads individual cases to trace where a search attempt goes wrong and which breakdowns are worth fixing.

*Want to see which step in the find-path most often broke in the posts we read?*

rows.question: Do Android users struggle to find photos more than iPhone users?
rows.restated: Do Android users struggle to find photos more than iPhone users?
rows.gap: the posts do not reliably say which phone people use, so there is no Android vs iPhone split
dropped: That said, the evidence does allow partial answers about where searches fail for the vaguely remembered photos group (115 cases).
rows.text:
**No — the study cannot tell whether Android users struggle more than iPhone users.** The posts do not reliably record device or platform, so there is no Android vs iPhone split to compare. [[analysis_method_flags|missing_cuts]]

For those cases we can say what details posts do and do not report: for example, what people remembered is reported in 192 of 331 cases and what they typed is reported in 76 of 331 cases, but phone type is not reported in a usable way. [[analysis_coverage|2.1]][[analysis_coverage|4.1]][[analysis_funnel|collected]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]][[analysis_method_flags|missing_cuts]]

My read is that comparing platforms would be misleading without device fields: any observed difference in public posts could reflect who posts, not who struggles. A likely reason is posts over-represent trouble and lack metadata about phones. This suggests product or research work should collect device info in interviews or instrumentation before concluding platform differences.

*Want to see what people actually typed when their search failed?*

rows.question: Has search got worse since Ask Photos launched?
rows.restated: Has Google Photos search quality declined since the Ask Photos feature launched?
rows.gap: the stories were not compared across time, so there is no before-and-after
rows.text:
I'm afraid the posts can't show whether search has worsened since Ask Photos launched — the public cases have no reliable before/after comparison, so they don't speak to change over time. [[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]][[analysis_method_flags|missing_cuts]]

What the evidence does show about vaguely remembered photos is that search itself first failed in about a quarter of the cases: in 31 of 115 cases the person typed a usable clue but the search did not bring up the photo. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]] A roughly similar number of cases — 38 of 115 — report that nothing went wrong and they found the photo. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

My read is that, for half-remembered photos, three distinct problems matter: the photo was already gone (about one in six cases), people never used search (about one in ten), and search returned results but the target was hard to spot (about one in ten). These proportions point to where improvements would help most if you want to help people with vague memories: better retrieval for short, usable queries; clearer result surfacing to help spotting; and non-search safeguards for lost photos. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=3@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=6@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

*Would you like to see the exact phrases people typed when they did use search?*

rows.question: Is Apple Photos search better than Google Photos search at finding old photos?
rows.restated: Is Apple Photos search better than Google Photos search at finding old photos?
rows.gap: the stories do not compare how well other photo apps search
rows.text:
I'm afraid the posts can't settle whether Apple Photos search is better than Google Photos search; the data contain only public accounts about Google Photos and no usable direct comparisons. [[analysis_method_flags|missing_cuts]]

That said, for old photos in Google Photos the study shows where searches most often fail: in the 115 cases where people only vaguely remembered a photo, about two in five of those posts were on X (49 cases) and about a quarter were YouTube comments (30 cases), which tells you where complaints are posted though not why. [[analysis_crosstab|core.source=youtube@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.source=x@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_sources|youtube]][[analysis_sources|x]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

What we can say from these cases is limited: only a minority of cases report whether metadata like date, place or faces were correct (only 3 of 115), so the posts rarely let us tell if missing or wrong metadata explains failures. [[analysis_coverage|0.2]] My read is that, lacking comparative data, the fairest conclusion is we cannot judge Apple versus Google from this evidence.

*Want to see exactly what people typed or what search showed them in these cases?*

rows.question: How deep do people scroll through search results before deciding?
rows.restated: How far down people scroll through search results before deciding whether they found the photo?
rows.gap: few public posts say anything about how far down the results they went — 2 of 115 stories do — so it is left for interviews with real users
dropped: What we can say from the posts is merely that some people do keep scrolling until they spot the photo and some stop after a few scrolls — the public-post evidence cannot settle which is more common or why.
rows.text:
**The public posts tell us almost nothing — only two of the 115 cases say how far people scrolled.** [[analysis_coverage|6.6]][[analysis_funnel|collected]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

Those two reports disagree — one says a few scrolls and the other says all the way down, so they point only to a handful of behaviours, not a pattern. [[analysis_crosstab|core.q:6.6=a_few_scrolls@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:6.6=exhaustive@photo_class:_all]] My read is that this is too small to say where people typically stop; interviews are needed to measure scrolling depth reliably. (The study deliberately followed the whole finding path so interviews can probe the missing steps.) [[analysis_funnel|collected]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]][[analysis_method_flags|interview_register]]

*Want to see the two posts that mention how far they scrolled?*

rows.question: How often does a wrong year act as a hard filter that hides the photo?
rows.restated: How often did people say that remembering the wrong year (a wrong date) acted as a hard filter that prevented the photo from appearing in Google Photos search results?
rows.gap: few public posts say anything about whether the system discarded the photo because one detail was wrong — 22 of 290 stories do — so it is left for interviews with real users
rows.text:
**The posts can't settle it — only 22 of the 290 cases say anything about whether one wrong detail caused the system to discard the photo, so we can't reliably measure how often a wrong year acted as a hard filter.** [[analysis_coverage|5.3]][[analysis_method_flags|interview_register]]

That said, among the 115 cases about a vaguely remembered photo, just a handful report a detail making the photo vanish or not matter: one person said adding more words made the photo disappear, and two said a small mistake did not matter — each reported in only one or two cases. [[analysis_crosstab|core.q:5.3=and_logic_shrinks_recall@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:5.3=soft_ok@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:5.3=soft_ok@photo_class:unclear]]

My read is that these public posts are too sparse and biased toward problems to tell us how often a wrong year specifically behaved like a hard filter; interviews with real users are needed to test whether a mismatched year commonly hides the photo and why. [[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]][[analysis_method_flags|public_selection_bias]][[analysis_method_flags|interview_register]]

*Want me to pull the exact phrases people typed when a detail made results disappear?*

rows.question: How many attempts do people make before they give up?
rows.restated: How many search attempts (queries or tries) do people make before they stop trying to find a photo?
rows.gap: two AI readers went through the stories separately and agreed too rarely on how long they kept trying to rely on it
dropped: That’s the direct, counted answer the posts provide; the evidence can’t reliably settle how long most people kept trying because the reviewers agreed too rarely on that detail.

My read is that the public posts mostly report outcomes (found quickly, found after a struggle, gave up) rather than a consistent log of repeated attempts, so counts about "how many tries before giving up" are sparse and uncertain.
rows.text:
**Exact count — in these 115 cases, four people gave up.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.outcome=abandoned_without_fallback@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

Only 30 of the 115 cases even say anything about how long they kept trying, and among those the posts record one try in 21 cases, a few minutes in 6, and an hour or more in 3. [[analysis_coverage|8.1]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:8.1=one_attempt@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:8.1=few_attempts_minutes@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.q:8.1=hour_or_more@photo_class:_all]]

*Want to see which exact phrases people typed when they tried first?*

rows.question: Why does Ask Photos fail most often?
rows.restated: Why does Ask Photos fail most often?
rows.text:
**Ask Photos most often fails because people type a good clue but the search still does not bring up the photo — about a quarter of the cases.** That is shown by the 31 of 115 cases where the first thing to go wrong was exactly that: a usable clue was entered but the photo did not appear in results [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]].

What the evidence shows is a clear bottleneck at the moment query meets results. The study followed each hunt step by step, and when a usable, correct clue was given the search failed to surface the target more often than any other single first failure (the next biggest first problems were deleted/missing photos and not using search) [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=3@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=6@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]. A likely reason is that half-remembered memories are short or imprecise, so queries are brief; when search must bridge from a short clue to many candidate photos it can fail to rank the target high enough to be noticed. My read is that improving how short, specific clues are interpreted or surfacing better disambiguation when results are broad would reach the largest group of frustrated cases.

I’m afraid the posts can’t settle why the engine missed each one internally — we only see what people wrote, not the system’s decision — so fixes should be tested with real users first [[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]][[analysis_method_flags|public_selection_bias]].

*Want to see the actual phrases people typed when search failed?*

rows.question: Since most failures happen because the photo was deleted, what should Google fix first?
rows.restated: If most finding the photo failures are due to the photo having been deleted, what should Google fix first?
rows.text:
**No — fixing deleted-or-never-backed-up photos should not be the first priority; better search that actually returns a usable result deserves priority because it was the first thing to go wrong in roughly a quarter of the cases.** [[analysis_opportunity|stage0]][[analysis_opportunity|stage5]]

The evidence — in the 115 cases about a vaguely remembered photo, the first break was that the person typed a usable clue but search did not bring up the photo in about a quarter of cases, while the photo being gone first came up in about one in six cases — a smaller share and one that better search cannot fix. [[analysis_opportunity|stage5]][[analysis_opportunity|stage0]]

My read is that improving how short, vague, or natural queries are matched would help the largest group here: if search surfaces the right candidate when someone supplies a usable clue, many hunts end quickly and avoid long scrolling or giving up. A likely reason is that these posts record recoverable photos where matching fails, so engineering work on relevance, query interpretation, and presenting high‑confidence candidates would yield the biggest practical win. This does not argue against better backup and recovery — deleted photos remain important — but the posts show it as a smaller first-point failure. [[analysis_opportunity|stage5]][[analysis_opportunity|stage0]][[analysis_method_flags|stage5_inferred]]

*Want to see exactly what people typed when search failed?*

rows.question: What share of utility-photo stories end with the person giving up?
rows.restated: What proportion of stories about practical photos end with the person giving up?
rows.gap: only 21 stories are about photos kept for the information in them (receipts, documents, notes) — too few (under 30) for a percentage, so only counts are given
dropped: That is the direct count the posts allow: four of the 21 cases about photos kept for information ended with the person giving up rather than finding the photo.
rows.text:
**Very few — in the 21 utility-photo cases, four people gave up.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=2@photo_class:utility]]

I'm afraid this is only a rough guide: 21 cases are fewer than thirty, so the study cannot sensibly turn that into a share of all such searches. [[analysis_method_flags|thin_core]]

My read is that when a photo with needed information is gone or simply not searchable, posters sometimes report giving up rather than settling for a similar photo; three of these 21 cases ended with finding the photo and eight first failed because the photo was already gone, which helps explain why some people stopped trying. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:utility]] This suggests improving backups or making gone-vs-present clearer could reduce giving up, but the posts can't settle how often that would help. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:utility]]

*Want to see the posts that say a receipt or document was gone or that the person gave up?*

rows.question: What share of stories about photos kept for both sentimental and practical reasons fail at search?
rows.restated: What proportion of stories about photos that were kept for both sentimental and practical reasons experienced a search failure (i.e., the finding the photo attempt first went wrong at some step rather than 'nothing went wrong')?
rows.gap: the stories hold nothing on how often this happens in the stories; no stories bear on this in detail; none of the stories is about photos kept both as memories and for the information in them, so nothing can be said about them
rows.text:
**The posts contain no cases about photos kept both for sentimental and practical reasons, so we cannot say what share of those cases fail at search.** The study found no cases that described a single photo being kept both as a memory and for the information in it, so there is nothing in the evidence to count or describe for that group [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=2@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:utility]][[analysis_method_flags|thin_core]][[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]]. 

What we can say from nearby groups is about photos kept purely as memories: in that set, roughly about a third of cases found the photo and roughly about a quarter first failed because someone typed a usable clue but search did not bring it up — small groups, so treat them as rough guides [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:sentimental]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:sentimental]]. My read is that if you want a usable product hypothesis, testing on photos held for mixed reasons should be done by interviews or targeted logs, because the public posts here simply don’t include them.

*Want me to pull the exact posts where people said they typed a usable clue but search didn’t show the photo?*

rows.question: How many core stories are there, and from how many different people?
rows.restated: How many stories about a vaguely remembered photo are in the dataset, and from how many different people did those stories come?
rows.text:
**There are 115 core cases, told by 109 different people.** [[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

That 115 is the set the study treats as the half‑remembered photo cases; the posts come from 109 distinct people who reported those cases. [[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

I'm afraid the posts can't tell us anything about how representative those people are or whether similar counts would hold for other groups, because these are public posts people chose to write. [[analysis_method_flags|proxy_not_success_rate]][[analysis_method_flags|public_selection_bias]]

*Want to see the raw posts behind those 115 cases?*

rows.question: How many core stories first go wrong because search did not understand or match what was typed?
rows.restated: How many stories about a vaguely remembered photo had their first finding the photo failure because search did not understand or match what the user typed?
rows.text:
**31 of the 115 core cases first went wrong because the person typed a usable clue but search did not bring up the photo.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

This means about a quarter of the half-remembered-photo cases reached for search with something usable to type and still failed to see the photo in results. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]] My read is that improving how short, specific queries are interpreted would reach the largest single group of failures here. A likely reason is that people often give brief clues (names, objects, short phrases) and the system either doesn't record that detail or doesn't surface matches for short queries; the posts themselves show users trying simple queries that returned nothing or unhelpful results. rows.text:
**The whole retrieval journey for a vaguely remembered photo runs from “photo present?” through motive, memory, search method, phrasing, matching, spotting and repeat attempts — and in about a quarter of the cases the first failure was that a correct clue was typed but search did not surface the photo.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]]

What happened along the path — first people checked whether the photo existed at all — in about one in six cases the photo was already gone (deleted, never backed up, or kept elsewhere). [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:_all]] Then they tried to find it because of some need (sharing, proof, nostalgia); that step is recorded but not counted separately. People then brought whatever they half-remembered: sometimes too little to form a query (one in twenty). [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=2@photo_class:_all]] Many turned to the search box; a minority never used search and only scrolled (about one in ten). [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=3@photo_class:_all]] When they typed usable clues, in roughly a quarter of cases the search did not bring up the photo. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]] Other times the photo was in results but hard to spot among similar images (about one in ten). [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=6@photo_class:_all]] A small handful of posts only say why they were looking, not what went wrong. [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=1@photo_class:_all]]

This suggests prioritising better ranking or recall for brief queries, and clearer ways to surface visually similar or borderline results so people can spot the target. Note the posts can’t show why a search missed internally, so we can’t say whether the gap is in understanding, indexing, or ranking. rows.question: What happens when people search for a pet photo and cannot find it?
rows.restated: What happens when people search for a pet photo and cannot find it?
rows.text:
**When people hunt for a vaguely remembered pet photo, about a quarter first fail because they typed a usable clue and search did not bring the photo.** [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=5@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

The evidence shows the rest of the ways the hunt breaks: about a third of such cases still found the photo, and the others first went wrong because the photo was already gone (about one in six), because they never used the search box (about one in ten), because the photo was in the results but hard to spot (about one in ten), or because they couldn't remember enough to search (about one in twenty). [[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=9@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=0@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=3@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=6@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_crosstab|core.primary_stage=2@photo_class:_all]][[analysis_funnel|stories:core]]

My read is that improving how short, concrete clues are interpreted would help the largest single group: if search returned the target when someone types a usable hint, many fewer hunts would stall. A likely reason is that people often supply brief pet-related terms (breed, place, "dog park", a name) and expect matching—when that fails they try other routes or quit. This suggests prioritising better recall-to-query matching and making results easier to scan. The posts can’t tell us why search missed internally or how often people retried, so we can’t say which technical fix would be most effective.
